04: Occlusion & Clipping - What's Visible?

This is the most computationally expensive step in the pipeline. For every edge we've extracted, we need to determine which portions are visible (in front of all geometry) and which are hidden (behind other triangles).

The Problem

Side View: Top View (projected): Camera looking down ┌───────┐ ↓ │ Box │ ═════ ═ ═ ═ ═══════ Edge ┌───┐ │ │ │Box│ └───────┘ └───┘ ═══════════════ Edge The edge passes behind the box. When projected to 2D: - Left part: VISIBLE (in front of box) - Middle part: HIDDEN (behind box) - Right part: VISIBLE (in front of box) We need to split the edge into 3 segments!

The Algorithm Overview

  1. Build a BVH for all extracted edges (LineObjectsBVH)
  2. For each triangle in the scene, find nearby edges using BVH
  3. For each edge-triangle pair, calculate the "hidden" portion
  4. Store hidden ranges as parametric coordinates [t0, t1]
  5. Merge overlapping hidden ranges
  6. Generate visible segments from gaps between hidden ranges

Step-by-Step Breakdown

1

LineObjectsBVH - A BVH for Lines

The library creates a custom BVH that stores line segments instead of triangles. This allows efficient spatial queries like "which edges are near this triangle?". 

// LineObjectsBVH extends MeshBVH with custom bounds calculation
// Each "primitive" is a Line3 instead of a triangle
class LineObjectsBVH extends MeshBVH {
    writePrimitiveBounds(nodeIndex, target) {
        const line = this.lines[nodeIndex];
        // Set bounding box from line start/end points
        target[0] = Math.min(line.start.x, line.end.x);
        target[1] = Math.min(line.start.y, line.end.y);
        // ... etc
    }
}
2

BVH Cast - Finding Edge-Triangle Pairs

We use edgesBvh.bvhcast(meshBvh) to efficiently find all pairs of (edge, triangle) that might interact. 

edgesBvh.bvhcast(meshBvh, matrixWorld, {
    intersectsRanges: (edgeOffset, edgeCount, triOffset, triCount) => {
        // Called when a group of edges might interact with a group of triangles
        // We check each combination in these ranges
    }
});
3

Back-Face Culling

Triangles facing away from the camera don't occlude anything. We skip them based on the material's side property. 

// Check if triangle faces up (toward camera) or down (away)
const faceUp = triangle.plane.normal.dot(UP_VECTOR) > 0;

// With FrontSide material, back-facing triangles don't occlude
if (side !== DoubleSide) {
    if (faceUp === (side === BackSide)) {
        continue;  // Skip this triangle
    }
}
4

Y-Bounds Check

Quick rejection: if the triangle is entirely below the edge, it can't occlude it. 

const highestTriangleY = Math.max(tri.a.y, tri.b.y, tri.c.y);
const lowestLineY = Math.min(line.start.y, line.end.y);

// Triangle entirely below the edge? Can't occlude!
if (highestTriangleY <= lowestLineY) {
    continue;
}
5

Trim to Beneath Triangle Plane

Only the portion of the edge that's below the triangle's plane can be occluded. We clip the edge to this portion.

Side View: Triangle plane ───────────────────────── ╲ Edge ═══════╳════════════ ╱ Only this part can be occluded! 
// trimToBeneathTriPlane returns the portion of the line
// that is below (behind) the triangle's plane
if (!trimToBeneathTriPlane(triangle, line, beneathLine)) {
    continue;  // Edge is entirely above triangle
}
6

Calculate Projected Overlap

Project both the edge and triangle to the XZ plane (flatten Y to 0). Find where the edge overlaps the triangle in 2D.

3D View: 2D Projection (XZ plane): Triangle Triangle /\ /\ / \ / \ / \ / \ /══════\════ Edge /══════\════ Edge /________\ /________\ ↑↑↑↑ Overlap region!

The algorithm creates a plane perpendicular to the edge, finds where triangle edges intersect this plane, and calculates the overlap range.

7

Store as Parametric Range

The overlap is stored as [t0, t1] where t is a value from 0 to 1 along the edge. t=0 is the start, t=1 is the end. 

// Convert overlap line back to parametric coordinates
const t0 = overlapStart.distanceTo(line.start) / lineLength;
const t1 = overlapEnd.distanceTo(line.start) / lineLength;

// Store in the hidden overlap map
hiddenOverlapMap[edgeIndex].push([t0, t1]);

Merging Overlapping Ranges

Multiple triangles might occlude the same edge. We need to merge overlapping ranges to avoid duplicate hidden segments.

Edge with multiple occluding triangles: Edge: ════════════════════════════════════════════ 0 1 Triangle A occludes: [0.2 ────── 0.5] Triangle B occludes: [0.4 ────── 0.7] Triangle C occludes: [0.65 ─ 0.75] After merging: [0.2 ───────────────── 0.75] Visible: [0 ── 0.2] [0.75 ── 1] Hidden: [0.2 ───────────────── 0.75]

The insertOverlap() function uses binary search to efficiently find the insertion point and merges with any overlapping existing ranges: 

function insertOverlap(result, overlapsTarget) {
    let [start, end] = result;

    // Binary search to find insertion point
    let left = 0, right = overlapsTarget.length;
    while (left < right) {
        const mid = (left + right) >>> 1;
        if (overlapsTarget[mid][0] <= start) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid;
        }
    }

    // Merge with any overlapping ranges
    for (let i = insertPoint; i < overlapsTarget.length; i++) {
        const [otherStart, otherEnd] = overlapsTarget[i];
        if (start <= otherEnd && end >= otherStart) {
            // Ranges overlap - merge them
            start = Math.min(otherStart, start);
            end = Math.max(otherEnd, end);
            deleteCount++;
        }
    }

    // Insert the merged range
    overlapsTarget.splice(insertPoint, deleteCount, [start, end]);
}

Generating Final Line Segments

After processing all triangles, each edge has a list of hidden ranges. We generate the final line segments: 

// For an edge with hidden ranges: [[0.2, 0.5], [0.7, 0.9]]

// Visible segments: [0, 0.2], [0.5, 0.7], [0.9, 1.0]
// Hidden segments:  [0.2, 0.5], [0.7, 0.9]

function generateLineSegments(edge, hiddenRanges) {
    const visible = [];
    const hidden = [];

    let lastEnd = 0;
    for (const [start, end] of hiddenRanges) {
        // Visible segment before this hidden range
        if (start > lastEnd) {
            visible.push(getSegment(edge, lastEnd, start));
        }
        // Hidden segment
        hidden.push(getSegment(edge, start, end));
        lastEnd = end;
    }
    // Final visible segment
    if (lastEnd < 1) {
        visible.push(getSegment(edge, lastEnd, 1));
    }

    return { visible, hidden };
}

The Complete Flow

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ bvhcastEdges() │ ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ │ │ INPUT: LineObjectsBVH (edges), MeshBVH (triangles), mesh │ │ │ │ edgesBvh.bvhcast(meshBvh): │ │ │ │ │ └─► for each (edgeRange, triangleRange) pair: │ │ │ │ │ └─► for each triangle in range: │ │ │ │ │ ├─► Transform triangle to world space │ │ ├─► Back-face culling check │ │ │ │ │ └─► for each edge in range: │ │ │ │ │ ├─► Y-bounds quick rejection │ │ ├─► Skip if edge lies on triangle │ │ ├─► Trim edge to beneath triangle plane │ │ ├─► Calculate projected XZ overlap │ │ ├─► Convert to parametric range [t0, t1] │ │ └─► Insert into hiddenOverlapMap (merge) │ │ │ │ OUTPUT: hiddenOverlapMap[edgeIndex] = [[t0,t1], [t2,t3], ...] │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

This is the Bottleneck!

This step accounts for ~95% of processing time in typical scenes. The complexity is roughly O(edges × triangles), though BVH acceleration makes it much faster in practice.

For very complex scenes, consider:

  • Using the VisibilityCuller to pre-filter meshes
  • Reducing mesh complexity where possible
  • Adjusting BVH parameters for better balance
